title: Journaling as practice
hookLine: writing as practice: an emperor wrote a book to himself, and the Stoics made writing a daily exercise
tomorrow: why did Benedict send monks around to check on the readers?

lines: A NOTES APP FULL OF HALF-THOUGHTS.
cards: A notes app fills up with half-thoughts: a screenshotted quote, a list that starts with eggs, one line typed at one in the morning and never opened again. Now another set of private notes.
The man writing them rules the Roman Empire, Marcus Aurelius. He's on the frontier with his army. He's writing in Greek, and not to anyone.
Tradition gives the book a plain title: to himself.

teach.b: He begins with thanks, person by person. From his grandfather Verus, he writes, he learned "good morals and the government of my temper."
Then his mother, his teachers, his adopted father, each with the thing they gave him. After that, the notes turn on himself. Reminders.

teach.h: BEGIN THE MORNING BY SAYING TO THYSELF.
teach.b: One opens: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself," and then lists the difficult people he'll meet that day, so he won't be surprised by them. He isn't writing a diary of what happened.
He's writing down what he already knows, again and again, until he lives it. That's the Stoic teaching inside the book.
For the Stoics, philosophy was training, and writing was one of the exercises. Epictetus, a teacher Marcus admired, told his students to keep the principles ready, to write them and read them daily.
Some modern scholars, like Pierre Hadot, read the whole book this way: not a set of thoughts for readers, but an emperor coaching himself, on paper.
So a journal in your rule can be more than a record of your day. It can be the place where you remind yourself who you mean to be, in your own hand, again tomorrow.

how: In the Stoic tradition, writing was a daily exercise: Marcus Aurelius's notes to himself open with thanks and return again and again to the same principles. On a personal rule, journaling is often a set time and place for a few lines.

games.q: your new journal is open. it's 10 pm and you've got five minutes. what would the Stoic way of journaling write?
o: one principle you mean to live by, said to yourself, plus who taught it to you.
a full record of everything that happened today, hour by hour.
a polished paragraph you could post tomorrow.
games.why: Marcus opened with thanks and then coached himself in the same few principles. It was training, not a log and not a post.

practice: Take a pen and write one line, the way Marcus began: from one person, what you learned. Then, under it, write when you'll write: a time of day and a place. For the rest of the sit, rest your hand on the page.
